The [[1984 Winter Olympics]], officially known as the XIV Olympic Winter Games, was a winter [[multi-sport event]] held in [[Sarajevo]], [[Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]], from 8 to 19 February 1984. A total of 1,272 athletes representing 49 [[National Olympic Committee]]s (NOCs) participated in 39 events from 10 different [[Olympic sports#Winter Sports|sports and disciplines]].<ref name="sarajevo 1984">{{cite web|title=Sarajevo 1984 Winter Olympics|url=http://www.olympic.org/en/content/Olympic-Games/All-Past-Olympic-Games/Winter/Sarajevo-1984/|work=Olympic.org|publisher=International Olympic Committee|access-date=21 July 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091004191243/http://www.olympic.org/en/content/Olympic-Games/All-Past-Olympic-Games/Winter/Sarajevo-1984/| archive-date= 4 October 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref> First time NOCs to enter were [[Egypt at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Egypt]], [[Monaco at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Monaco]], [[Puerto Rico at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Puerto Rico]], [[Senegal at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Senegal]], and [[British Virgin Islands at the 1984 Winter Olympics|British Virgin Islands]].<ref name="sarajevo 1984" />

Seventeen NOCs won at least one medal and, among these, eleven secured at least one gold medal. For the first time since its debut at the [[1968 Winter Olympics]], [[East Germany at the 1984 Winter Olympics|East Germany]] topped the gold medal count with nine, three more than the [[Soviet Union at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Soviet Union]], which had led this count in the past three Games. The Soviet delegation won the most overall medals (25), including the most silvers (10) and bronzes (9). The host nation, [[Yugoslavia at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Yugoslavia]], collected its first-ever medal at the Winter Olympics: a silver by [[Alpine skiing at the 1984 Winter Olympics|alpine skier]] [[Jure Franko]] in the [[Alpine skiing at the 1984 Winter Olympics|men's giant slalom]].<ref name="Jure Franko">{{cite news|last=Callahan|first=Tom|title=Sport: Something to Shout About|url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,921553,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101029154626/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,921553,00.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 29, 2010|access-date=23 July 2010|newspaper=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|publisher=Time Inc.|date=28 February 1984}}</ref> This was the third time that the Winter Olympics host team failed to win a gold medal, after France in [[1924 Winter Olympics|1924]] and Switzerland in [[1928 Winter Olympics|1928]].<ref>{{cite web|title=1924 Chamonix|url=http://www.olympic.ca/en/games/winter-olympics/1924-chamonix/#Medals|work=Olympic.ca|publisher=[[Canadian Olympic Committee]]|access-date=9 October 2010|archive-date=21 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321103654/https://olympic.ca/games/1924-chamonix/#Medals|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=1928 St. Moritz|url=http://www.olympic.ca/en/games/winter-olympics/1928-st-moritz/#Medals|work=Olympic.ca|publisher=[[Canadian Olympic Committee]]|access-date=9 October 2010|archive-date=21 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321103754/https://olympic.ca/games/1928-st-moritz/#Medals|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Austria at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Austrian]] athletes secured a single medal—a bronze in men's alpine skiing downhill—in what is the nation's worst ever result at the Winter Games.<ref>{{cite news|last=Waha|first=Eric|title=Austrian skiers hit by weltuntergangsstimmung|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=WYM0AAAAIBAJ&sjid=m6cEAAAAIBAJ&pg=1701,2379676|access-date=23 July 2010|newspaper=[[Anchorage Daily News]]|date=20 February 1984|agency=Associated Press}}{{Dead link|date=July 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
In contrast, [[Czechoslovakia at the Olympics|Czechoslovakia]] and [[Finland at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Finland]]'s performances in Sarajevo were historical bests, after collecting a total of six and thirteen medals, respectively.<ref name="CZE">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Czechoslovakia|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/TCH/|access-date=21 July 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100618021315/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/TCH/| archive-date= 18 June 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref><ref name="FIN">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Finland|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/FIN/|access-date=6 August 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100817010635/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/FIN/| archive-date= 17 August 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref>
Finnish cross-country skier [[Marja-Liisa Kirvesniemi|Marja-Liisa Hämäläinen]] was responsible for three of her NOC's four gold medals with a sweep of victories in the women's individual events, and contributed to the bronze in the team relay event.<ref name="Kirvesniemi">{{cite web|title=Marja-Liisa Kirvesniemi |url=http://www.olympic.org/en/content/olympic-athletes/all-athletes/athletes-ka-to-km/-marja-liisa-kirvesniemi-/ |work=Olympic.org |publisher=International Olympic Committee |access-date=23 July 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100814200254/http://www.olympic.org/en/content/Olympic-Athletes/All-Athletes/Athletes-KA-to-KM/-Marja-Liisa-Kirvesniemi-/ |archive-date=14 August 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
These Games also witnessed the best result by a [[Canada at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Canadian team]] since the [[1960 Winter Olympics]], thanks mostly to the achievements of [[Speed skating at the 1984 Winter Olympics|speed skater]] [[Gaétan Boucher]].<ref name="Gaetan Boucher">{{cite news|last=Farber|first=Michael|title=Canada stands tall – thanks to Boucher and Orser|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ftEyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=O-8FAAAAIBAJ&pg=1031,4543098|access-date=23 July 2010|newspaper=[[Ottawa Citizen]]|date=20 February 1984|agency=Southam News|location=Ottawa|archive-date=21 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321103654/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ftEyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=O-8FAAAAIBAJ&pg=1031%2C4543098|url-status=live}}</ref> His wins in the men's 1,000 and 1,500 metres, and a third place in the 500 metres, earned Canada's two gold medals and three of its four medals.<ref name="Gaetan Boucher" />
[[Sweden at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Sweden]] secured four golds for the first time since [[1948 Winter Olympics|St. Moritz 1948]],<ref name="SWE">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Sweden|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/SWE/|access-date=3 October 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100916064133/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/SWE/| archive-date= 16 September 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref> of which three were obtained by cross-country skiers [[Gunde Svan]] and [[Thomas Wassberg]]. Svan and Wassberg won the men's 15&nbsp;km and 50&nbsp;km, respectively, and also clinched the first place in the team relay.<ref name="svan-wassberg">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Sweden cross-country skiing at the 1984 Sarajevo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/SWE/winter/1984/CCS/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417070057/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/SWE/winter/1984/CCS/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=3 October 2010}}</ref> Svan was also awarded with a silver and bronze medals, thus contributing half of his NOC's medal tally.<ref>{{cite news|title=U.S. Olympic team gets its Phil at the end|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=1g4iAAAAIBAJ&sjid=hqcFAAAAIBAJ&pg=5796,8237944&dq=thomas+wassberg+gunde+svan&hl=en|access-date=3 October 2010|newspaper=[[Reading Eagle]]|date=20 February 1984|agency=Associated Press|page=20|archive-date=21 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321103655/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=1g4iAAAAIBAJ&sjid=hqcFAAAAIBAJ&pg=5796%2C8237944&dq=thomas+wassberg+gunde+svan&hl=en|url-status=live}}</ref>
For the third consecutive Winter Olympics, [[Great Britain at the 1984 Winter Olympics|Great Britain]]'s sole medal was a gold at a [[Figure skating at the 1984 Winter Olympics|figure skating]] event,<ref name="GBR">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Great Britain|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/GBR/|access-date=21 July 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100628142824/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/GBR/| archive-date= 28 June 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref> this time in ice dancing by [[Jayne Torvill]] and [[Christopher Dean]], who received the first-ever set of perfect scores in their free program routine.<ref>{{cite news|title=British skaters perform perfectly|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=E7MjAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nyQEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6677,5655244&dq=jure+franko&hl=en|access-date=23 July 2010|newspaper=[[Times-News (Hendersonville, North Carolina)|The Times-News]]|location=Hendersonville, N.C.|date=15 February 1984|agency=[[Associated Press]]|page=15|archive-date=21 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321103729/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=E7MjAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nyQEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6677%2C5655244&dq=jure+franko&hl=en|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{see also|Olympic medal table}}
The medal table is based on information provided by the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) and is consistent with IOC convention in its published medal tables. The table uses the [[Olympic medal table]] sorting method. By default, the table is ordered by the number of gold medals the athletes from a nation have won, where a nation is an entity represented by a [[National Olympic Committee]] (NOC). The number of silver medals is taken into consideration next, and then the number of bronze medals.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ostlere |first1=Lawrence |date=11 August 2024 |title=Olympic medal table: USA beat China to top spot at Paris 2024 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2580716.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240812015233/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2594580.html |archive-date=12 August 2024 |access-date=12 August 2024 |work=[[The Independent]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Araton |first1=Harvey |date=18 August 2008 |title=A Medal Count That Adds Up To Little |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321004238/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |archive-date=21 March 2023 |access-date=25 July 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> If teams are still tied, equal ranking is given and they are listed alphabetically by their [[List of IOC country codes|IOC country code]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cons |first1=Roddy |date=10 August 2024 |title=What happens if two countries are tied in the Olympic medal table? Tiebreaker rules explained |url=https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240811152350/https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |archive-date=August 11, 2024 |access-date=11 August 2024 |work=[[Diario AS]] |language=en-us}}</ref>
